title: PS-1 Using GPS enabled smart ear-tags to determine cow movement predictability and associations with cow/calf interactions and production metrics
content:
Abstract
Precision agriculture technologies are advancing exponentially and include the evolution of GPS location ear-tags that are used to monitor various livestock metrics such as location and feeding behaviors. These types of technologies are perhaps more commonly utilized than other developing biosensors, yet the large quantities of high-resolution data that are generated makes it difficult for cattle producers to capitalize on their full potential. A better understanding of how these data can be used to guide management decisions in an applied setting is necessary. The objective of this pilot project was to determine the predictability of cow movement, the association with cow-calf interactions, and if these behaviors associate with meaningful production metrics. A total of 39 commercial cows from the University of Wyoming Beef Unit herd were first fitted with 701x (n = 26 xTPro tags; n = 13 xTLite tags) GPS enabled smart ear-tags before being turned out to pasture prior to calving. Calves (n = 40) were fitted with the 701x xTLite tags at the time of calving. Cow body weights and body condition score were evaluated during the monitoring period (March – May) and calf weight was recorded at calving, branding, and weaning to provide production metrics to evaluate alongside location and behavior data. To evaluate if age of dam plays a role in location behavior and cow-calf interactions, the cows were assigned to one of three categories based on age (young, 4 – 5 yr, n = 12; mature, 6 – 8 yr, n = 14; old, 9 – 13 yr, n = 13). Open-sourced R-based scripts were then developed to process GPS location data and conduct spatial statistical analysis to determine if the data is meaningfully connected to production outcomes. Results indicate cows that have more predictable day to day movement have more interactions with their calves (r = 0.43, P < 0.01) independent of age of dam. Independent of age, more predictable cows that are having more interactions with their calves are likely to have calves with an increased daily weight gain (r = 0.46, P = 0.06). Data collected during this pilot project indicates a potential application of these types of precision technologies in deciphering meaningful production metrics that could be utilized in management decisions. Future analyses will include longer study periods in more expansive grazing scenarios which could provide more robust and applicable data for cow-calf producers.
